claims.reviewer_notes: Hook claim of the published long-form (first long-form draft, 2026-11-03). Britannica: ancient Greek mechanical device used to calculate and display astronomical information; Nature 2006: unique Greek geared device that calculated and displayed celestial information and predicted lunar and solar eclipses.
claims.text: A geared bronze machine that predicted eclipses existed in the ancient world about two thousand years ago.

claims.location: Off Antikythera, Greece; National Archaeological Museum, Athens
claims.objects: sponge divers, Roman-era merchant ship, corroded bronze lump
claims.reviewer_notes: First long-form draft, 2026-11-03; script chapter 1. Britannica: remains recovered in 1901 from the wreck of a trading ship near Antikythera, now on display in the National Archaeological Museum in Athens. Nature 2006: discovered in 1901 in a Roman shipwreck; its 82 fragments survive in the museum. NAM collection page: the Mechanism (X15087) is held in the Collection of Metalwork, Room 38.
claims.text: Sponge divers found the wreck off Antikythera in 1900, recovered the corroded lump in 1901, and its fragments are now held at the National Archaeological Museum in Athens.

claims.objects: corroded bronze lump with an embedded gear wheel
claims.reviewer_notes: Final long-form script wording, approved by Kristian 2026-11-05 ('The museum's Valerios Stais studied it after the gear was spotted'). The four description sources do not state the 1902 spotting, so the claim is supported by the secondary explainer src_thesea, which records that on 17 May 1902 the museum's director, archaeologist Valerios Stais, saw a gearwheel embedded in a broken piece. Single-secondary-source KNOWN claim; flagged here rather than overstated.
claims.text: In 1902 a gear was spotted inside the corroded lump, and the museum's Valerios Stais studied it.

claims.reviewer_notes: First long-form draft, 2026-11-03; final script chapter 2. Nature 2006 Figure 1 caption: the 82 fragments that survive in the National Archaeological Museum in Athens. Scientific Reports 2021: now split into 82 fragments, including 30 corroded bronze gearwheels. Britannica: radiographic images showed the remaining fragments contained 30 gear wheels.
claims.text: What survives is 82 fragments containing 30 bronze gear wheels.

claims.reviewer_notes: First long-form draft, 2026-11-03 ('Britannica puts at 100 BCE, give or take thirty years'). Britannica: manufacture currently dated to 100 BCE, give or take 30 years. Nature 2006: lettering dated to the second half of the second century BC, implying construction during 150-100 BC, consistent with the Britannica range.
claims.text: The mechanism was built around 100 BCE, give or take thirty years.

claims.objects: largest gear with 223 teeth, Saros eclipse dial
claims.reviewer_notes: Final long-form script chapter 2, 2026-11-05. Nature 2006: 'Of the periods, 223 is the Saros eclipse cycle'; the mechanism predicted lunar and solar eclipses on the basis of Babylonian arithmetic-progression cycles. Britannica: the large lower dial shows months with a likelihood of a solar or lunar eclipse, based on the 18.2-year Saros eclipse cycle.
claims.text: The largest gear has 223 teeth, and 223 lunar months make the Saros cycle of about eighteen years, whose dial predicted solar and lunar eclipses.

claims.objects: front zodiac dial, Moon-phase ball, back spiral dials
claims.reviewer_notes: Final long-form script chapter 2, 2026-11-05. Britannica: front dial with pointers for the Sun and Moon in the zodiac and a half-silvered ball for lunar phases; upper back dial five-turn spiral showing the 235 lunations of the Metonic cycle (almost exactly 19 years); subsidiary four-year dial for the Panhellenic games including the Olympics; lower dial Saros eclipse cycle. Nature 2006: the device calculated and displayed celestial information, particularly the phases of the Moon and a luni-solar calendar.
claims.text: The front dials showed the Sun and Moon moving through the zodiac and the Moon's phases, and the back dials carried the 235-month Metonic spiral, the Saros spiral, and a four-year dial for the Panhellenic Games.

claims.objects: X-ray CT scanner, bronze fragments with Greek inscriptions
claims.reviewer_notes: Final long-form script chapter 3, 2026-11-05. Nature 2006: high-resolution X-ray tomography of the surviving fragments, doubling the number of deciphered inscriptions. Scientific Reports 2021 confirms Microfocus X-ray CT in 2005 of the 82 fragments. Heritage 2021: new inscriptions unread for more than 2000 years were revealed mainly with X-ray micro-focusing tomography, and approximately 3500 letters and symbols have been deciphered, which supports the script's 'more than 3,000 characters'. Britannica: the surviving Greek inscriptions indicate clearly much of the device's astronomical and calendrical purpose, which supports the 'instruction manual' characterisation.
claims.text: X-ray computed tomography in 2005 revealed hidden gears and inscriptions invisible to the naked eye, reading more than 3,000 characters of Greek text that describe the dials and cycles, like an instruction manual.

claims.reviewer_notes: Gap wording settled in scripts/antikythera_master_blueprint.md (mtime 2026-11-04; accuracy annotation 3: use 1,400, not the blueprint's 1,500, and not the early draft's 'a thousand years'). Precision caveat: both cited sources state the gap as 'a millennium' (Britannica: no other geared mechanism of such complexity until medieval cathedral clocks a millennium later; Nature 2006: more complex than any known device for at least a millennium afterwards). The script's 'about 1,400 years' is the gap to the 14th-century cathedral clocks; it is kept as the reviewed wording and this note records that the sources support 'at least a millennium' rather than the exact 1,400 figure.
claims.text: Nothing comparably complex appears again for about 1,400 years, until the great clocks of medieval cathedrals.

claims.reviewer_notes: First long-form draft, 2026-11-03; final script chapter 4: 'The builder is UNKNOWN, and any video that gives you a name is guessing.' UNKNOWN by definition: no source names a builder, so no source is linked. The absence of evidence is the claim; do not attach a source to fill the gap.
claims.text: No inscription on the mechanism names its builder, and no ancient text describes the workshop that made it or the person who paid for it.

claims.debate_summary: The surviving gear trains and inscriptions point toward a planetary display, but the planetary gears themselves were never recovered, so the full cosmos display is inferred rather than found.
claims.objects: UCL cosmos reconstruction model, planetary gear rings
claims.position_a: The UCL team argues the inscriptions and surviving gear trains describe a complete cosmos display with planetary rings, and their 2021 model matches all the surviving evidence.
claims.position_b: The planetary gears were never recovered and nearly all the relevant parts are missing, so the full planetary display remains an inference, not a surviving fact.
claims.reviewer_notes: First long-form draft, 2026-11-03 (theory two: a model of the cosmos); final script chapter 3 tiers the 2021 UCL cosmos model DEBATED, not settled fact, because the planetary gears were never recovered. Scientific Reports 2021 is the model itself; Nature 2006 documents what physically survives; Britannica states the inscriptions imply a possible planetary display but nearly all the relevant parts are missing.
claims.text: A 2021 University College London reconstruction models the mechanism as a display of the whole cosmos, with planetary gears.

claims.reviewer_notes: Final long-form script chapter 2, 2026-11-05. Britannica: originally in a case about the size of a shoebox. src_thesea: the wooden case is estimated at about 34 by 18 by 9 centimetres, roughly the size of a large shoebox. Caveat: Nature 2006 gives the uncertain overall size as 315 x 190 x 100 mm, consistent with the script's rounded figures.
claims.text: The surviving fragments fit together into a wooden case roughly 34 centimetres long, 18 wide, and 9 deep, about the size of a shoebox.

sources.notes: Checked 2026-11-15 against the live article (published 2009-02-19, updated 2026-09-17). Confirms: recovered 1901 from a trading ship that sank in the first half of the 1st century BCE near Antikythera; manufacture dated to 100 BCE, give or take 30 years; fragments contain 30 gear wheels; no other geared mechanism of such complexity until medieval cathedral clocks a millennium later; shoebox-sized case; Greek inscriptions indicating the astronomical/calendrical purpose; front dial Sun/Moon in the zodiac and half-silvered Moon-phase ball; back dials Metonic 235 lunations over 19 years, four-year Panhellenic Games dial, Saros 18.2-year eclipse cycle; inscriptions imply a possible planetary display but nearly all the relevant parts are missing. Does NOT mention Stais, the 1902 gear spotting, the 82-fragment count, the 223-tooth gear, or the 2005 X-ray CT work, so it is never the sole source for those claims.
sources.title: Antikythera mechanism

sources.notes: Freeth et al., Nature 444, 587-591 (2006), published 30 November 2006. Checked 2026-11-15. Confirms: unique Greek geared device constructed around the end of the second century BC; discovered in 1901 in a Roman shipwreck; technically more complex than any known device for at least a millennium afterwards; high-resolution X-ray tomography of the surviving fragments, doubling the number of deciphered inscriptions; mechanism predicted lunar and solar eclipses on the basis of Babylonian arithmetic-progression cycles; 223 is the Saros eclipse cycle; lettering dated to the second half of the second century BC, implying construction 150-100 BC; Figure 1 caption: the 82 fragments that survive in the National Archaeological Museum in Athens; case of uncertain overall size 315 x 190 x 100 mm.
sources.title: Decoding the ancient Greek astronomical calculator known as the Antikythera Mechanism

sources.notes: Freeth et al., Scientific Reports 11, 5821 (2021), published 12 March 2021, UCL Antikythera Research Team. Checked 2026-11-15. Confirms: mechanism challenged researchers since its discovery in 1901; now split into 82 fragments, only a third of the original survives, including 30 corroded bronze gearwheels; Microfocus X-ray Computed Tomography (X-ray CT) in 2005 of the 82 fragments; the front remained deeply controversial due to loss of physical evidence; the paper builds a new model of a cosmos display (nine concentric rings: Moon, Nodes, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Date) that matches the surviving evidence. It is a model, not a recovered object, which is why the cosmos-display claim is tiered DEBATED.
sources.title: A Model of the Cosmos in the ancient Greek Antikythera Mechanism

sources.notes: The museum's own collection page, checked 2026-11-15. Confirms the Antikythera Mechanism (inventory X15087) is held in the Collection of Metalwork, Room 38, among the finds from the Shipwreck of Antikythera, and calls it the most significant scientific instrument of antiquity. Used here as the archival anchor that the surviving fragments are held at the National Archaeological Museum in Athens. It does not state dates, gear counts, or the 1902 spotting, so it is never the sole source for those claims.
